pulls.title: Add `context_settings` parameter to `CliRunner.invoke`
pulls.body:
This PR adds a `context_settings` parameter to `CliRunner.invoke()`, allowing tests to pass context-specific settings to the command's `Context`.

`CliRunner.invoke()` passes its extra keyword arguments to the `Context` of the command, except `color`: its own `color` parameter takes that name. `context_settings` solves this collision. And now a test can set what its terminal supports, as well as the `color` of the context in the same call.

With this addition, I can now test cases that were previously difficult or impossible to cover, such as verifying how the command behaves with different `Context` settings.

This was proposed 5 years ago in #2110 but at that time this change was evaluated as niche. Since then, we did a lot of color handling improvements in Click (#3505, #3653, #3739) which added a lot of color-related tests, so this is no longer a niche concern.

For evidence, I used the new `context_settings` parameter to extend and simplify existing checks. See `test_prompt_and_confirm_ansi_respects_color` and `test_tempfile_pager_handles_ansi`.

pulls.title: Add `Parameter.spec` and deprecate `human_readable_name`
pulls.body:
This a follow up of https://github.com/pallets/click/pull/3821 , where I introduced a new `Option.get_help_spec` utility.

While discussing this change, [I realized we had 3 aspects](https://github.com/pallets/click/pull/3821#issuecomment-5510226827) of a parameter for 3 different audiences:
- `decls`: what the developer provide to its argument or option
- `spec`: what the user see in `--help` and what it provide to the CLI
- `name`: what is used internally in Click to identify that argument or option

And I just realize now that I can harmonize this vocabulary in the whole Click codebase with a small effort. This PR is that effort.

For illustration, here is the value of each property as taken from the documentation:

| | `@click.argument('recipe')` | `@click.option('-g', '--gluten-free/--no-gluten-free')` |
|---|---|---|
| `decls` | `('recipe',)` | `('-g', '--gluten-free/--no-gluten-free')` |
| `spec` | `RECIPE` | `--gluten-free` |
| `name` | `recipe` | `gluten_free` |
| `opts` | `['recipe']` | `['-g', '--gluten-free']` |
| `secondary_opts` | `[]` | `['--no-gluten-free']` |

The effects this PR has:
- Rename `Parameter.human_readable_name` to `Parameter.spec` and deprecate the former
- Make `get_help_spec` more generic by moving it from `Option` to `Parameter`
- Document `opts` and `opts `

And as such targets 8.6.0.

I still did not pushed my luck too much by proposing a rename of the `.name` property into `.id` or `.uid` as in [my original comment](https://github.com/pallets/click/pull/3821#issuecomment-5510226827) to keep this proposal reasonable. 😇

This add `DeprecationWarning` that detect when `Parameter`, `Argument` or `Option` gets a `name` that will be not allowed in the future 9.0.0 release:
- a parameter that is not a Python identifier (check against `str.identifier`)
- a parameter that is a Python keyword (check against `keyword.iskeyword`)
- an option name that is nor lower-cased

This PR also copy the majority of tests that were originally proposed in #3827, so the behavior of the `name` is locked down and frozen. This will prevent tweaking or introducing regressions during the full 8.x cycle.

This PR also inaugurate the 8.6.0 release on `main`.

issues.title: [rejected AI] `IntRange`/`INT`/`FLOAT` leak `TypeError` and `OverflowError` instead of refusing with `BadParameter`
issues.body:
**Versions:** click 8.1.7 (tested), still present in 8.5.0.
**Component:** `click/types.py`, `_NumberParamTypeBase.convert` — so `click.INT`,
`click.FLOAT`, `click.IntRange`, `click.FloatRange` and every subclass.
**Python:** 3.14 (the three exception classes are CPython's own, so the version only
changes which values reach `int()`; the bug is version-independent).

## What happens

`_NumberParamTypeBase.convert` wraps the numeric cast in a `try` that catches **only**
`ValueError`:

```python
    def convert(self, value, param, ctx):
        try:
            return self._number_class(value)
        except ValueError:
            self.fail(
                _("{value!r} is not a valid {number_type}.").format(
                    value=value, number_type=self.name
                ),
                param,
                ctx,
            )
```

`int()` and `float()` raise two further classes for values `convert` is documented to
accept:

* **`TypeError`** — a value the constructor does not take at all: `None`, a `list`, a
  `dict`, an arbitrary object. `int(None)` →
  `TypeError: int() argument must be a string, a bytes-like object or a real number, not 'NoneType'`.
* **`OverflowError`** — `int(float("inf"))` →
  `OverflowError: cannot convert float infinity to integer`.

Both leave `convert` unchanged, so they reach the caller as themselves rather than as the
`click.BadParameter` that `ParamType.fail` exists to raise.

`ParamType`'s own docstring names the call shape as supported — "*It must be able to
convert a value if the `ctx` and `param` arguments are `None`. This can occur when
converting prompt input.*" — and every other `ParamType.convert` in the library refuses
bad input by calling `self.fail`.

## Why it matters

`Parameter.type_cast_value` passes a non-`None` value straight to `ParamType.__call__`,
which passes it to `convert`. A `default=` the type cannot convert therefore ends the
program with a traceback and **exit status 1 and no output**, where every other conversion
failure produces a usage message and **exit status 2**:

```python
import click

@click.command()
@click.option("--n", type=click.IntRange(0, 100), default=[1, "2"])
def cli(n):
    click.echo(f"n={n!r}")

cli()
```

```
$ python cli.py
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
TypeError: int() argument must be a string, a bytes-like object or a real number, not 'list'
$ echo $?
1
```

The same happens with `default=float("inf")` (`OverflowError`), with a `default` read from
`ctx.default_map`, and with any object a caller installs as a default. A user who wrote
`except click.ClickException` — the documented way to handle a CLI error — does not catch
either.

## Minimal fix

Catch the two classes the cast can raise:

```diff
-        except ValueError:
+        except (ValueError, TypeError, OverflowError):
             self.fail(
                 _("{value!r} is not a valid {number_type}.").format(
                     value=value, number_type=self.name
                 ),
                 param,
                 ctx,
             )
```

`fail` renders `{value!r}`, so the message is already useful for a non-numeric value:
`"<object object at 0x…> is not a valid integer range."`.

With the patch, the example above prints

```
Usage: cli.py [OPTIONS]
Try 'cli.py --help' for help.

Error: Invalid value for '--n': '[1, '2']' is not a valid integer range.
```

and exits 2.

## Compatibility

The library's own suite is unchanged: **532 passed, 22 skipped, 1 xfailed** before and
after the patch (`tests/`, click 8.1.7's tree; `tests/test_basic.py` does not collect on
current pytest for an unrelated reason and is excluded from both runs).

The behaviour that changes is exactly the one that was a traceback: no currently-passing
conversion starts failing, because a value that reaches the new `except` clause was
previously raising out of `convert` rather than returning.

## Not affected

A **string** input is not a way to trigger this: `int(str)` raises only `ValueError`, which
is already caught, so `"abc"`, `""`, `"1e3"` and an over-long digit literal all produce
`BadParameter` correctly today.

issues.title: Atomic file writes replace the original file when the context exits with an exception
issues.body:
## Summary

When using `click.open_file(..., atomic=True)`, an exception raised inside the file context still causes the temporary file to replace the original destination file.

This means a failed write can overwrite previously valid data with incomplete content.

## Steps to reproduce

Run this code:

```python
import click
from pathlib import Path
import tempfile

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    target = Path(directory) / "important.txt"
    target.write_text("ORIGINAL DATA")

    try:
        with click.open_file(str(target), "w", atomic=True) as f:
            f.write("PARTIAL DATA")
            raise RuntimeError("Simulated failure")
    except RuntimeError:
        pass

    print(target.read_text())
```

## Actual behavior

The output is:

```text
PARTIAL DATA
```

The original file is overwritten despite the exception.

## Expected behavior

The output should be:

```text
ORIGINAL DATA
```

The original file should remain unchanged when the operation fails.

## Technical investigation

In `src/click/_compat.py`, `_AtomicFile.__exit__()` calls:

```python
self.close(delete=exc_type is not None)
```

However, `_AtomicFile.close()` ignores the `delete` argument and always executes:

```python
os.replace(self._tmp_filename, self._real_filename)
```

Therefore, the temporary file replaces the original even when an exception occurs.

## Impact

Applications using atomic file writing may lose previously valid file contents when an exception occurs during a write.


## Environment

- Operating system: macOS
- Python version: 3.14.7
- Click source commit: `2247b35ea1c47c727d7a06e51fa280e12a863ff6`
- API: `click.open_file(..., atomic=True)`

## Reproducibility

Successfully reproduced locally using the repository source code.

issues.title: [rejected AI] `Choice.shell_complete` Unicode case-folding mismatch under `case_sensitive=False`
issues.body:
#### Outline
When `case_sensitive=False`, `Choice.normalize_choice` normalizes choice values using `.casefold()`. However, `Choice.shell_complete` normalizes the user's `incomplete` input string using `.lower()`. In Unicode, `.lower()` and `.casefold()` diverge for non-ASCII characters (e.g. `'ß'.lower() == 'ß'`, while `'ß'.casefold() == 'ss'`). Consequently, completing a word containing such characters fails completely because the prefix comparison is performed between a casefolded choice and a lowercased prefix.

#### Steps to Reproduce
```python
import click

choice = click.Choice(["GROSS", "GROß"], case_sensitive=False)
cmd = click.Command("cmd")
ctx = click.Context(cmd)
param = click.Option(["--type"], type=choice)

completions = choice.shell_complete(ctx, param, "groß")
print("Completions returned:", [c.value for c in completions])
assert len(completions) > 0, "No completions returned for valid prefix 'groß'!"
```

#### Traceback / Output
```
Completions returned: []
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test_choice.py", line 10, in <module>
    assert len(completions) > 0, "No completions returned for valid prefix 'groß'!"
AssertionError: No completions returned for valid prefix 'groß'!
```

#### Expected Behavior
`shell_complete` should normalize `incomplete` using `.casefold()` so that Unicode case-folding matches choices consistently.

#### Root Cause Analysis
In `src/click/types.py`, lines 508–514:
```python
str_choices = [self.normalize_choice(choice, ctx) for choice in self.choices]
if self.case_sensitive:
    matched = (c for c in str_choices if c.startswith(incomplete))
else:
    incomplete = incomplete.lower()
    matched = (c for c in str_choices if c.lower().startswith(incomplete))
```
`normalize_choice` has already applied `.casefold()` to every element of `str_choices`. Using `incomplete.lower()` creates an algorithmic mismatch against the casefolded choices, causing `.startswith()` to return `False`.

#### Proposed Fix
```diff
--- a/src/click/types.py
+++ b/src/click/types.py
@@ -509,8 +509,8 @@ class Choice(ParamType[_ValueT_co], t.Generic[_ValueT_co]):
         if self.case_sensitive:
             matched = (c for c in str_choices if c.startswith(incomplete))
         else:
-            incomplete = incomplete.lower()
-            matched = (c for c in str_choices if c.lower().startswith(incomplete))
+            incomplete = incomplete.casefold()
+            matched = (c for c in str_choices if c.startswith(incomplete))
 
         return [CompletionItem(c) for c in matched]
```

#### Regression Test
```python
def test_choice_case_insensitive_casefold_completion():
```

issues.title: [rejected AI] Short options with attached `=` (e.g. `-u=admin`) corrupt the parsed value to include the `=` sign
issues.body:
#### Outline
Standard POSIX CLI conventions and Python's `argparse` allow passing short options with attached arguments using `=` (e.g. `-u=admin` or `-f=file.txt`). In Click, passing `-u=admin` when `-u` is declared as an option taking a value results in `u` being assigned the string `'=admin'` with a leading equals sign. Furthermore, if `-v` is a boolean flag, passing `-v=foo` fails with `NoSuchOption: No such option: -=` rather than reporting that the option does not accept a value.

#### Steps to Reproduce
```python
import click
from click.testing import CliRunner

@click.command()
@click.option("-u", type=str)
def cli(u):
    click.echo(f"u: {u!r}")

runner = CliRunner()
res = runner.invoke(cli, ["-u=admin"])
print("Actual output:", res.output.strip())
assert res.output.strip() == "u: 'admin'", f"Expected 'admin' but received {res.output.strip()}"
```

#### Traceback / Output
```
Actual output: u: '=admin'
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test_short_opt.py", line 12, in <module>
    assert res.output.strip() == "u: 'admin'", f"Expected 'admin' but received {res.output.strip()}"
AssertionError: Expected 'admin' but received u: '=admin'
```

#### Expected Behavior
The attached `=` sign should be recognized as the option/argument delimiter, assigning `u = 'admin'` (matching `argparse` and GNU/POSIX semantics). If the option is a flag, Click should raise `BadOptionUsage: Option '-v' does not take a value.`

#### Root Cause Analysis
In `src/click/parser.py`:
1. `_process_opts` splits `arg` on `=` to test for attached values (`long_opt, explicit_value = "-u", "admin"`).
2. It attempts `self._match_long_opt("-u", explicit_value, state)`, which raises `NoSuchOption` because `"-u"` is in `_short_opt`, not `_long_opt`.
3. In `except NoSuchOption:`, it invokes `self._match_short_opt(arg, state)` with the original string `arg = "-u=admin"`.
4. Inside `_match_short_opt`:
   ```python
   if option.takes_value:
       if i < len(arg):
           state.rargs.insert(0, arg[i:])
           stop = True
       value = self._get_value_from_state(opt, option, state)
   ```
   `i` is 2, so `arg[i:]` is `"=admin"`. Click inserts `"=admin"` into `state.rargs`, and `_get_value_from_state` consumes it directly.

#### Proposed Fix
```diff
--- a/src/click/parser.py
+++ b/src/click/parser.py
@@ -407,11 +407,19 @@ class _OptionParser:
                 # Any characters left in arg?  Pretend they're the
                 # next arg, and stop consuming characters of arg.
                 if i < len(arg):
-                    state.rargs.insert(0, arg[i:])
+                    opt_val = arg[i:]
+                    if opt_val.startswith("="):
+                        opt_val = opt_val[1:]
+                    state.rargs.insert(0, opt_val)
                     stop = True
 
                 value = self._get_value_from_state(opt, option, state)
 
+            elif i < len(arg) and arg[i] == "=":
+                raise BadOptionUsage(
+                    opt, _("Option {name!r} does not take a value.").format(name=opt)
+                )
+
             else:
                 value = UNSET
```

#### Regression Test
```python
def test_short_option_with_attached_equals(runner):
    @click.command()
    @click.option("-u", type=str)
    def cli(u):
        click.echo(f"u: {u}")

    result = runner.invoke(cli, ["-u=admin"])
    assert result.exit_code == 0
    assert result.output.strip() == "u: admin"


def test_short_flag_with_attached_equals_errors(runner):
    @click.command()
    @click.option("-v", is_flag=True)
    def cli(v):
        pass

    result = runner.invoke(cli, ["-v=foo"])
    assert result.exit_code == 2
    assert "Option '-v' does not take a value" in result.output
```

- Python version: 3.10 / 3.11 / 3.12 / 3.13 / 3.14
- Click version: 8.0+ / 8.6.0a0 (`main`)

```
Serialized dict: {'exists': False, 'file_okay': True, 'dir_okay': True, 'writable': False, 'readable': True, 'allow_dash': False, 'param_type': 'Path', 'name': 'path'}
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test_info.py", line 7, in <module>
    assert "executable" in info, "'executable' missing from to_info_dict()"
AssertionError: 'executable' missing from to_info_dict()
```

```python
    'param_type': 'Path',
    'name': 'path',
    'exists': False,

    'writable': False,
```

issues.title: [rejected AI] `HelpFormatter.write_dl`: raises `TypeError: Expected two columns for definition list` on empty sequence
issues.body:
#### Outline
Calling `HelpFormatter.write_dl(rows)` with an empty sequence `rows = []` crashes with `TypeError: Expected two columns for definition list`. An empty definition list should be a valid no-op. Because `write_dl` lacks an empty-sequence guard, internal callers (`format_options`, `format_commands`) and third-party extensions are forced to maintain redundant `if records:` guards to avoid crashing.

#### Steps to Reproduce
```python
from click.formatting import HelpFormatter

formatter = HelpFormatter()
formatter.write_dl([])
```

#### Traceback
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 4, in <module>
    formatter.write_dl([])
  File "src/click/formatting.py", line 246, in write_dl
    raise TypeError("Expected two columns for definition list")
TypeError: Expected two columns for definition list
```

`write_dl([])` should return cleanly without appending to the buffer.

```python
rows = list(rows)
widths = measure_table(rows)
if len(widths) != 2:
    raise TypeError("Expected two columns for definition list")
```

```diff
--- a/src/click/formatting.py
+++ b/src/click/formatting.py
@@ -241,6 +247,8 @@ class HelpFormatter:
                             second column.
         """
         rows = list(rows)
+        if not rows:
+            return
         widths = measure_table(rows)
```

issues.title: [rejected AI] `wrap_text` collapses paragraphs into a single line when blank lines contain whitespace
issues.body:
#### Outline
When formatting docstrings or command help texts with `wrap_text(text, preserve_paragraphs=True)`, empty lines that contain whitespace characters (e.g. trailing spaces or tabs on an otherwise blank line) fail to trigger paragraph flushing. Instead of separating paragraphs, Click treats the whitespace line as an indented continuation of the active paragraph, strips the line to `""`, and joins the surrounding paragraphs with a space. This causes multi-paragraph documentation to be collapsed into a single run-on paragraph with extraneous spacing.

#### Steps to Reproduce
Run the following script:

```python
from click.formatting import wrap_text

# Blank line contains 3 spaces
help_text = "First paragraph of instructions.\n   \nSecond paragraph of instructions."
wrapped = wrap_text(help_text, preserve_paragraphs=True)

print("Result:\n" + repr(wrapped))
assert "\n\n" in wrapped, "Paragraph separation was lost!"
```

#### Traceback / Output
```
Result:
'First paragraph of instructions.     Second paragraph of instructions.'
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test_wrap.py", line 8, in <module>
    assert "\n\n" in wrapped, "Paragraph separation was lost!"
AssertionError: Paragraph separation was lost!
```

#### Expected Behavior
Lines containing only whitespace should be recognized as paragraph boundaries. The output should preserve the double newline between paragraphs:
```
'First paragraph of instructions.\n\nSecond paragraph of instructions.'
```

#### Root Cause Analysis
In `src/click/formatting.py`, lines 87–96:
```python
for line in text.splitlines():
    if not line:
        _flush_par()
        indent = None
    else:
        if indent is None:
            orig_len = term_len(line)
            line = line.lstrip()
            indent = orig_len - term_len(line)
        buf.append(line)
_flush_par()
```
When `line` consists only of spaces (e.g. `"   "`), `if not line:` evaluates to `False`. The loop enters the `else:` branch, measures `indent`, sets `line = ""` via `line.lstrip()`, and appends `""` to `buf`. Because `buf` is not flushed, the next paragraph's lines are appended to the same buffer and joined with `" "`.

#### Proposed Fix
```diff
--- a/src/click/formatting.py
+++ b/src/click/formatting.py
@@ -88,6 +88,12 @@ def wrap_text(
         if not line:
             _flush_par()
             indent = None
+        elif line.isspace():
+            if buf:
+                _flush_par()
+                indent = None
+            else:
+                buf.append("")
         else:
             if indent is None:
                 orig_len = term_len(line)
```

#### Regression Test
```python
def test_wrap_text_whitespace_blank_lines():
    from click.formatting import wrap_text
    text = "First paragraph.\n   \nSecond paragraph."
    wrapped = wrap_text(text, preserve_paragraphs=True)
    assert "\n\n" in wrapped
    assert wrapped.split("\n\n") == ["First paragraph.", "Second paragraph."]
```

#### Environment
- Python version: 3.10 / 3.11 / 3.12 / 3.13 / 3.14
- Click version: 8.5.x / 8.6.0a0 (`main`)

issues.title: [rejected AI] Case-insensitive Choice completion misses Unicode case-folding matches
issues.body:
### Description

`Choice` uses `casefold()` for case-insensitive conversion, but `shell_complete()` lowercases the incomplete value and compares it with `lower()`. This makes completion fail for Unicode case-folding expansions.

For example, `Choice(["ẞ"], case_sensitive=False)` accepts `"ß"` during conversion because both values case-fold to `"ss"`, but completion for the incomplete value `"ß"` returns no suggestion because `"ss".lower().startswith("ß")` is false.

```python
from click import Choice

choice = Choice(["ẞ"], case_sensitive=False)
assert choice.convert("ß", None, None) == "ẞ"

# A completion callback using this Choice receives incomplete="ß".
# It currently produces no completion item, even though the normalized choice is "ss".
```

The relevant implementation is `Choice.shell_complete()` in `src/click/types.py`; it uses `lower()` while `normalize_choice()` uses `casefold()`.

### Expected behavior

Case-insensitive shell completion should use the same Unicode-aware normalization as conversion and return the normalized `"ss"` suggestion for incomplete `"ß"`.

### Actual behavior

No completion item is returned.

### Environment

- Latest `main` at the time of filing
- Python 3.12+
- Click shell completion

I searched existing issues and pull requests for Unicode casefolding and Choice completion and did not find a matching report. A regression test covering `ẞ`/`ß` would prevent this from recurring.

issues.title: [rejected AI] Envvar for multiple=True + nargs>1 silently drops incomplete trailing tokens
issues.body:
﻿When an option uses `multiple=True` and `nargs > 1`, an environment-variable value whose whitespace-split token count is **not a multiple of `nargs`** is accepted with exit code 0, and the trailing incomplete group is **silently discarded**.

The same values on the CLI are rejected (e.g. `Got unexpected extra argument`). Non-multiple `nargs > 1` options already reject incomplete envvar values with `BadParameter` (`Takes N values but M were given.`). The `multiple=True` path should do the same instead of truncating.

Root cause: `Option.value_from_envvar()` calls `batch()`, which uses `zip(..., strict=False)` and drops remainder tokens.

## Reproduction

```python
import click
from click.testing import CliRunner

runner = CliRunner()

@click.command()
@click.option("--arg", nargs=2, multiple=True)
def cli(arg):
    click.echo(repr(arg))

# Envvar: silently drops "c"
r = runner.invoke(cli, [], auto_envvar_prefix="TEST", env={"TEST_ARG": "a b c"})
print(r.exit_code, r.output.strip())
# Actual: 0  "(('a', 'b'),)"

# CLI: rejects the extra token
r2 = runner.invoke(cli, ["--arg", "a", "b", "c"])
print(r2.exit_code)
print(r2.output)
# Actual: exit 2, "Got unexpected extra argument (c)"
```

Also reproduces with `envvar="ARG"` and `env={"ARG": "a b c"}`.

With five tokens (`"a b c d e"`), the result is `(('a', 'b'), ('c', 'd'))` — `e` is silently discarded.

## Expected behavior

Envvar parsing should raise `BadParameter` (same family of arity error used for non-multiple `nargs` envvars), instead of silently dropping tokens and exiting 0.

## Environment

- Python version: 3.12.10
- Click version: main @ 36baa15 (8.5.1 unreleased)

issues.title: [rejected AI] count=True ignores non-zero default when counting flags
issues.body:
<!--
This issue tracker is a tool to address bugs in Click itself. Please use
GitHub Discussions or the Pallets Discord for questions about your own code.

Replace this comment with a clear outline of what the bug is.
-->

When an option uses `count=True` with a non-zero `default`, each occurrence of the flag counts from **0** instead of from the configured default. Passing fewer flags than the default can therefore produce a value **lower than the default** (or leave `default=1` unchanged when the flag is passed once).

This differs from `argparse.ArgumentParser` with `action="count"`, which increments relative to the default (for example `default=3` plus one flag occurrence yields `4`).

<!--
Describe how to replicate the bug.

Include a minimal reproducible example that demonstrates the bug.
Include the full traceback if there was an exception.
-->

```python
import argparse
import click
from click.testing import CliRunner

# argparse (expected-aligned behavior)
p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
p.add_argument("-v", action="count", default=3)
print("argparse no flags", p.parse_args([]).v)        # 3
print("argparse one flag", p.parse_args(["-v"]).v)    # 4
print("argparse two flags", p.parse_args(["-vv"]).v)  # 5

# click
@click.command()
@click.option("-v", count=True, default=3)
def cli(v):
    click.echo(v)

runner = CliRunner()
print("click no flags", runner.invoke(cli, []).output.strip())       # 3
print("click one flag", runner.invoke(cli, ["-v"]).output.strip())   # 1  ← bug
print("click two flags", runner.invoke(cli, ["-vv"]).output.strip()) # 2  ← bug
```

Root cause appears to be in `click/parser.py`, where the count action always starts from `0`:

```python
state.opts[self.dest] = state.opts.get(self.dest, 0) + 1
```

Once a command-line count is present, `consume_value()` takes that value and never applies the option default as a baseline.

<!--
Describe the expected behavior that should have happened but didn't.
-->

Expected (argparse-compatible): command-line counts are **additive** on top of the option default.

| Invocation | Expected | Actual (Click) |
|---|---|---|
| `(none)` | `3` | `3` |
| one `-v` | `4` | `1` |
| `-vv` | `5` | `2` |
| `-vvv` | `6` | `3` |

With `default=1`, a single flag occurrence should yield `2`, but currently yields `1` (same as omitting the flag).

Environment:

- Python version: 3.12.10
- Click version: 8.5.1.dev0 (main)

issues.title: [rejected AI] Literal mutable default silently accumulates mutations across CliRunner.invoke() calls with a pass-through ParamType
issues.body:
**AI disclosure:** this was investigated and written with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic). I independently reproduced it against a fresh clone of `main` myself before filing.

## Summary

A literal mutable default (e.g. `default=[]`, `default={}`) on an `Option` silently accumulates mutations across separate command invocations within one process, when combined with a `ParamType` whose `convert()` validates and returns the value unchanged (e.g. `type=click.UNPROCESSED`, or any custom type handling structured data like a JSON/dict param).

This is the classic Python mutable-default-argument trap — Click's own docs correctly recommend `default=list`/`default=dict` (a callable factory) as the safe pattern, and that path genuinely works. But a literal mutable default only gets protected from this trap by accident, when the default type-coercion path happens to stringify/rebuild the value (e.g. plain `--items` with no `type=` routes through `StringParamType`). Nothing actually copies the default before handing it to the callback.

## Reproduction

```python
import click
from click.testing import CliRunner

@click.command()
@click.option("--items", type=click.UNPROCESSED, default=[])
def cmd(items):
    items.append("x")
    click.echo(f"len={len(items)}")

runner = CliRunner()
print(runner.invoke(cmd, []).output.strip())  # len=1
print(runner.invoke(cmd, []).output.strip())  # len=2  <- same list object, not reset
print(runner.invoke(cmd, []).output.strip())  # len=3
```

Confirmed against current `main`: `id(items)` is identical across all three calls.

## Root cause

`Parameter.get_default()` (`click/core.py:2445-2476`) only special-cases *callable* defaults (`if call and callable(value): value = value()`, line 2473) — a literal default value is returned as-is, no copy. `type_cast_value`/`consume_value` never copy it either before it reaches the callback.

The reason a plain `default=[]` doesn't normally show this (and why it's easy to miss): Click's type-inference (`click/types.py` `_guess_type`) routes an untyped list default through `StringParamType`, which effectively rebuilds the value rather than passing the same object through. `type=click.UNPROCESSED` (documented, and the natural choice for custom structured-data types) explicitly opts out of that coercion — and loses the incidental protection along with it.

## Scope

Only manifests in a long-running process that invokes the same command repeatedly — a test suite using `CliRunner.invoke()` in a loop, a REPL-style tool, or any host process embedding Click commands. A single-shot CLI invocation never notices, since the process exits after one call.

Checked `gh search issues --repo pallets/click` for "mutable default", "default list shared", "get_default copy" — no matching prior report found.

Happy to put together a PR (something like: deep-copy a literal mutable default via `copy.deepcopy` in `get_default()`, mirroring the protection callable defaults already get) if this is confirmed worth fixing.

issues.title: Terminal escape-sequence injection in error messages
issues.body:
### Summary
Click is vulnerable to terminal escape-sequence injection because command-line tokens are interpolated raw into error messages that are written to the user's terminal without control-character filtering.

Verified on Click at commit https://github.com/pallets/click/commit/36baa15ff831b939a22bc527cd76ce653ef6f66d (8.5.1.dev0).
### Details
Click reflects unsanitised `argv` tokens into error output at two locations:

`click/src/click/core.py:1391` interpolates the raw tokens:

```python
ngettext(
    "Got unexpected extra argument ({args})",
    "Got unexpected extra arguments ({args})",
    len(args),
).format(args=" ".join(map(str, args)))
```

`click/src/click/types.py:1013` interpolates the raw filename:

```python
self.fail(
    f"'{format_filename(value)}': {e.strerror}",
    param,
    ctx,
)
```

Both reach the terminal through `echo()` (`utils.py:324`), whose only sanitisation is `strip_ansi()`. That sanitisation does not apply here, for two independent reasons:

- `should_strip_ansi()` (`_compat.py:499-506`) returns `not isatty(stream)`, so stripping is skipped entirely when the stream is a terminal.
- `_ansi_re` (`_compat.py:19`) is `r"\033\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]"`, which matches only 7-bit CSI. OSC, DCS, APC, 8-bit C1 (`\x9b`), `ESC c`, and bare C0 controls (`\r`, `\b`) are never stripped.

Consequently an attacker-supplied token is delivered to the terminal emulator byte-for-byte. This permits window-title spoofing (OSC 0), forged program output by moving the cursor and overwriting earlier lines (CSI / `\r`), attacker-controlled hyperlinks under arbitrary anchor text (OSC 8), and — on terminals where clipboard write is enabled — silently staging a shell command in the victim's clipboard for their next paste (OSC 52).

### PoC
1. Create a file named `poc.py` with the following content:
```python
import click
 
@click.command()
@click.option("--f", type=click.File("r"))
def cli(f):
    click.echo("ok")
 
if __name__ == "__main__":
    cli()
```
2. Run the Python script:
```
python3 poc.py $(echo -en '\x0dOVERWRITTEN USING ESCAPE SEQUENCE')
```
3. Observe that the raw escape bytes reach the terminal.

### Suggested Remediation
Apply `!r` at both reflection sites, matching the convention already used everywhere else in the codebase:

```diff
diff --git a/src/click/core.py b/src/click/core.py
index de129ec..5c6c9de 100644
--- a/src/click/core.py
+++ b/src/click/core.py
@@ -1391,7 +1391,7 @@ class Command:
                     "Got unexpected extra argument ({args})",
                     "Got unexpected extra arguments ({args})",
                     len(args),
-                ).format(args=" ".join(map(str, args)))
+                ).format(args=" ".join(map(repr, args)))
             )
 
         ctx.args = args
diff --git a/src/click/types.py b/src/click/types.py
index 0eb8462..2d9e30f 100644
--- a/src/click/types.py
+++ b/src/click/types.py
@@ -1010,7 +1010,7 @@ class File(ParamType[t.IO[t.Any]]):
             return f
         except OSError as e:
             self.fail(
-                f"'{format_filename(value)}': {e.strerror}",
+                f"'{format_filename(value)!r}': {e.strerror}",
                 param,
                 ctx,
             )
diff --git a/tests/test_arguments.py b/tests/test_arguments.py
index fea48cc..5a0e3e3 100644
--- a/tests/test_arguments.py
+++ b/tests/test_arguments.py
@@ -76,7 +76,7 @@ def test_nargs_err(runner):
 
     result = runner.invoke(copy, ["foo", "bar"])
     assert result.exit_code == 2
-    assert "Got unexpected extra argument (bar)" in result.output
+    assert "Got unexpected extra argument ('bar')" in result.output
 
 
 def test_bytes_args(runner, monkeypatch):
```

Found by [OSTIF](https://ostif.org/) using AI with their own harness.
Manually verified, fixed, and reported by [Shielder](https://www.shielder.com/).

issues.title: Nightly "Stress" jobs run the normal test suite; the stress tests never execute
issues.body:
The four `test_stress_*` tests do not run in CI, or anywhere else. The nightly Stress jobs run the ordinary test suite with those tests deselected.

### Why

`pyproject.toml:91` deselects them globally:

```toml
addopts = "-m 'not stress'"
```

`pyproject.toml:178-183` defines an environment that overrides it, and that environment is correct:

```toml
[tool.tox.env.stress]
commands = [["pytest", "-v", "--tb=short", "-x", "-m", "stress",
             "--basetemp={env_tmp_dir}", "--override-ini=addopts=", ...]]
```

But `nightly.yaml:27-29` does not run `stress`. It runs `stress-py3.14` and `stress-py3.14t`, which are listed in `env_list` at `pyproject.toml:150`:

```yaml
- {name: Stress 3.14,     python: '3.14',  tox: stress-py3.14}
- {name: Stress 3.14t,    python: '3.14t', tox: stress-py3.14t}
- {name: Stress Mac 3.14t, python: '3.14t', tox: stress-py3.14t, os: macos-latest}
```

tox's TOML source does not decompose factors for `[tool.tox.env.<name>]`, so `stress-py3.14` does not inherit from `[tool.tox.env.stress]`. It is generated from `env_run_base` instead.

### Reproducing

With tox 4.52.0 (the version in `uv.lock:1370`) and tox-uv:

```
$ tox config -e stress-py3.14
commands = pytest -v --tb=short --basetemp=<workdir>/stress-py3.14/tmp
base     = tool.tox.env_run_base

$ tox config -e stress
commands = pytest -v --tb=short -x -m stress --basetemp=<workdir>/stress/tmp --override-ini=addopts=
```

`stress-py3.14` gets neither `-m stress` nor `--override-ini=addopts=`, so it inherits `-m 'not stress'` and runs the normal suite. The `py3.14` factor *is* honoured (`base_python = py3.14`), which is what makes the name look like it worked; the `stress-` prefix matches nothing.

No warning is emitted — stderr is empty, and `tox -vv config -e stress-py3.14` produces no mention of an unmatched name. `tox config -e totally-made-up-env` does fail with "provided environments not found in configuration file", so the name resolves specifically because `env_list` contains it.

### Not running anywhere

- `tests/test_stream_lifecycle.py:495` `test_stress_thread_pool_with_exit`
- `tests/test_stream_lifecycle.py:512` `test_stress_logging_sequential_invocations`
- `tests/test_stream_lifecycle.py:528` `test_stress_gc_between_invocations`
- `tests/test_utils/test_echo_via_pager.py:231` `test_stress_echo_via_pager_exception_cleanup`

Happy to open a PR if you have a preference on the fix — the matrix could name `stress`, or the environments could be defined per-Python.
